standard.title: Values of water
standard.description: the economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic value of water for people, including First Nations Australians
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have completed K01 and K02 — they can classify water resources, trace water movement connecting places, and explain distribution and sustainability. Those nodes treat water primarily as a physical and economic resource. This standard introduces the cultural, spiritual and aesthetic dimensions of water value, which require a different conceptual lens.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic value of water for people, including First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: Framework of water values
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic values of water and give an example of each.
nodes.minimum_width: Students define each value type and provide at least one concrete example.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain each of the four value types (economic, cultural, spiritual, aesthetic) and provide examples drawn from Australian and Asian contexts, recognising that a single water body may hold multiple value types simultaneously.
wider: Examine how the four value types can conflict — e.g. a river's economic value (irrigation) may conflict with its spiritual value for First Nations communities — and consider how such conflicts are mediated
Compare how values attributed to water differ across cultures — e.g. the aesthetic value of a waterfall in Japanese culture vs an Australian National Park listing for the same feature type
Explore how a value type can be 'discovered' or recognised — e.g. aesthetic value formalised through World Heritage listing
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish the four value types — particularly conflating cultural and spiritual, or treating economic value as the only 'real' value — will struggle to explain First Nations relationships to Country/water in node 2, which requires understanding non-economic values as primary rather than supplementary.

response_modes.reason: The economic/non-economic distinction needs explicit scaffolding. Many students default to economic explanations. A structured reasoning approach that requires students to explain each value type on its own terms — not as a secondary consideration after economics — addresses this.
Widening to cases where non-economic values are primary (spiritual significance, aesthetic listing) gives students examples where the framework applies without defaulting to economic framing.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The four-value framework is a transferable analytical tool applicable to any landscape feature, not just water. Students who develop genuine fluency with all four types have a more complete geographical toolkit and are better prepared for the liveability standards (K05–K08) where similar multi-value analysis appears.
success_criteria: Names and distinguishes economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic values of water, providing a concrete example for each.
Identifies a water body or waterway that holds more than one type of value and explains how each applies.

nodes.label: First Nations Australians and multilayered water values
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the multilayered meanings of water for First Nations Australians — material, cultural and spiritual — using specific examples of rivers, waterways, waterholes or other water features.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain that water features hold material, cultural and spiritual significance for First Nations Australians, supported by at least one specific example.
nodes.typical_width: Students discuss the multilayered meanings (material, cultural and spiritual wellbeing) associated with rivers, waterways, waterholes, human-made wells, seas, lakes, soaks and springs for First Nations Australians, explaining how these meanings are connected to Country/Place and to social identity.
wider: Examine the Mutitjulu Waterhole — its material significance as a water source, cultural significance in Anangu Tjukurpa, and spiritual significance as a living Dreaming site — as a case study of integrated multilayered meaning
Research how water-sharing protocols and custodianship responsibilities reflect the relationship between First Nations peoples and water features
Examine how dispossession and land management changes have affected First Nations Australians' relationship with water features, and current efforts to restore cultural access
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat First Nations water values as merely 'cultural enrichment' (supplementary to economic value) will not be able to explain why water management decisions that prioritise economic value can cause profound harm to First Nations communities. This understanding is foundational to K07 (cultural connectedness to place).

response_modes.reason: Students need scaffolding to understand that material, cultural and spiritual dimensions are simultaneously present — not alternatives — in First Nations relationships to water. A case study approach where all three dimensions are traced in the same water feature makes this concrete.

Using multiple water feature types (waterhole, river, coastal waterway, soak) broadens understanding beyond a single exemplar and reveals that multilayered water values operate across all water forms, not just iconic sites.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The richness of First Nations water relationships connects to Country/Place, Dreaming, custodianship and rights — all of which extend into K07. Students who develop genuine understanding here are better positioned to analyse liveability, belonging and place identity for diverse groups.
success_criteria: Explains at least two dimensions of water significance (material, cultural, spiritual) for First Nations Australians using a specific water feature as an example.
Describes the relationship between water and Country/Place identity for at least one First Nations community.

nodes.label: Economic value of water: irrigation and food production
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the economic value of water for irrigation-based communities and industries, using a comparison between an Australian and an Asian example.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the economic value of water for one irrigation case study.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine and compare places in Australia and a country in Asia that have economies and communities based on irrigation — e.g. the Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area in NSW and the Mekong Delta in Vietnam — identifying similarities and differences in how irrigation shapes economic and community life.
wider: Analyse the virtual water embedded in food exports from irrigation regions — calculate the 'water cost' of traded agricultural products and consider what this means for water sustainability
Compare the economic value of irrigation water with the economic value of water for urban use — how are competing economic values prioritised and by whom?

Examine historical case studies where irrigation dramatically changed regional economies and societies (e.g. development of the Ord River, transformation of the MIA) and evaluate the costs and benefits

response_modes.reason: Comparing Australian and Asian irrigation cases prevents students from treating economic water value as a purely domestic story. The Mekong Delta case also shows water's economic value in a different national and cultural context.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Australia-Asia comparison called for in the elaborations is an opportunity to build genuine comparative geographical analysis, examining what is common across irrigation economies and what reflects local context — this is a transferable skill for the rest of the Geography 7 curriculum.
success_criteria: Explains the economic role of water in an irrigation-based region using a specific Australian example.
Compares at least one similarity and one difference in how irrigation shapes economic life in an Australian and an Asian context.

nodes.label: Aesthetic and cultural value of water: heritage and tourism
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the aesthetic and cultural value of water features through examples of World Heritage or national park listings in Australia and Asia.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the aesthetic or cultural value of one water-related heritage or protected site.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine bays, rivers, waterfalls or lakes in Australia and in countries of Asia that have been listed as World Heritage sites or national parks for their aesthetic and cultural value, explaining what features generate these values and how listing reflects them.
wider: Examine how aesthetic value of a water feature generates economic value through tourism — is aesthetic value independent of or connected to economic value?

Investigate the spiritual significance of water in an Asian culture (e.g. the Ganges in Hindu practice, sacred lakes in Tibetan Buddhism) and compare the nature of that significance with Australian First Nations examples
Analyse how the criteria for World Heritage listing reflect particular cultural frameworks for 'outstanding universal value' and consider whose values are centred

response_modes.reason: The elaborations explicitly call for Asian examples. Widening to include spiritual significance in Asian cultures (not just aesthetic/heritage) builds fuller understanding of non-economic water values across diverse cultural contexts.

success_criteria: Explains the aesthetic or cultural value of a water feature in Australia or Asia, including why it has been formally recognised through listing or protected status.
Describes at least one way aesthetic or spiritual value of water differs between two cultural contexts.

nodes.label: Integration: multiple values in tension and context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students explain the economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic value of water for people — applying the four-value framework to a specific case and recognising where values coexist or conflict.
nodes.minimum_width: Students apply at least two value types to a specific water-related context, explaining each value's source and how they relate.
nodes.typical_width: Students produce an integrated explanation of a specific water feature or water management case that identifies economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic values, explains how these are expressed by different groups, and considers whether and how they coexist or conflict.
wider: Analyse a water management decision (e.g. a proposed dam, a river restoration project) using the four-value framework — identify which values are advanced, which are compromised, and for which communities

Apply the framework to a case involving First Nations Australians and non-Indigenous water users — e.g. the Darling/Baaka River, the Daintree, or a local river — to assess whose values inform decision-making and whose are marginalised

response_modes.reason: The four value types are taught separately but the descriptor requires students to apply them together. The integration node practises the analytical move of seeing a single water context through all four lenses simultaneously.

success_criteria: Applies at least three of the four value types to a specific water feature or management case, explaining each.
Identifies at least one point of tension between different values held by different groups for the same water feature.
